column1: # Prose mentions of identifiers whose definitions are gone — DISPOSITIONED.
# Read by tools/renamed_names_left_in_prose.py. Rows silence a candidate it
# would otherwise ask about.
#   name <TAB> hash <TAB> category <TAB> note
# `hash` identifies the MENTION BY ITS CONTENT — the first 12 hex of a sha256
# over the line's whitespace-normalized text. Not the file, not the line number.
# WHY CONTENT AND NOT LOCATION, with this repo's own proof: kiss_byte_match.rs
# named `arch_from_code` in the PRESENT TENSE as a live precondition — stale —
# and a rewording turned it into a record of what that precondition used to
# point at — historical. Same name, same file, changed only by editing the
# sentence. A row keyed on (name, file) would silence every future mention of
# that name in that file, INCLUDING one a later edit reintroduces in the present
# tense: a 282-entry allowlist arriving one row at a time, through the door
# marked "disposition". Keyed on content, a disposition expires when its subject
# changes and only when its subject changes.
# Owed to Fuel, who saw it before anyone had written a row — when the migration
# was three rows rather than "re-disposition everything, which nobody does".
# category is one of:
#   historical   the prose is ABOUT the rename or about prior behaviour.
#                Renaming it destroys the record.
#   pinned       the document describes the code AS OF a revision.
#                Renaming it makes the document false.
# `stale` is NOT a category. A stale mention means the current thing and names
# the old one; it gets FIXED, never recorded here.
# Taxonomy owed to Fuel, who produced it independently while triaging a 296-file
# prefix drop: twelve prose mentions of names that no longer existed, twelve of
# twelve correct to leave.
# RATCHETED BOTH WAYS. A row whose name is named nowhere also fails the check —
# a suppression that has stopped suppressing is worse than no suppression,
# because it reads like coverage.
